titre: Domestic Work Enters International Labor Law Only in 2011
accroche: Until 2011, work done in a home remained, in most countries, outside labor law. An ILO convention changes the rule.
contenu_vulgarise:
Geneva, June 16, 2011. At its hundredth session, the International Labour Conference adopts, by 396 votes in favor, 16 against, and 63 abstentions, Convention No. 189 of the International Labour Organization on decent work for domestic workers. The Organization itself presents it as a historic text.

## A Kind of Work Left Outside Labor Law

Until this convention, domestic work, household help, child care, or care for the elderly, largely escaped international labor instruments. The convention's preamble acknowledges this by calling it "undervalued and invisible," "mainly carried out by women and girls." The reason lies in the very nature of this work: it is carried out in a private home and not in an establishment, which long took it, in many countries, outside the scope of the laws that organize ordinary labor law, labor inspection included. The convention lays down the opposite principle. Its Article 3 requires each state that ratifies it to ensure domestic workers the same fundamental principles as other employees: freedom of association and collective bargaining, elimination of forced labor, abolition of child labor, non-discrimination. Its Article 6 guarantees them fair terms of employment, like workers generally.

The text goes down to practical detail: a contract, preferably written, specifying the employer, housing, hours, pay, and conditions of departure (Article 7); for people recruited in one country to work in another, a written job offer even before crossing the border (Article 8); protection against abuse, harassment, and violence (Article 5).

## A Ratification That Begins with Uruguay

On April 26, 2012, the Uruguayan Parliament approves the convention and becomes the first country to ratify it. In line with the standard rule for ILO conventions, entry into force follows the second ratification by one year: Convention No. 189 takes effect on September 5, 2013.

On paper, the convention creates almost no right that did not already exist for other employees: freedom of association, rest, protection against violence appeared in older texts of the International Labour Organization. What it changes is to write in black and white that a person who works in a home has no reason to be excluded from the rules that protect those who work elsewhere. That a separate text was needed to say so, ninety-two years after the creation of the International Labour Organization in 1919, shows how much this work remained, in practice, outside the common scope.

repere.texte: Considering that domestic work continues to be undervalued and invisible and is mainly carried out by women and girls, many of whom are migrants or members of disadvantaged communities and who are particularly vulnerable to discrimination in respect of conditions of employment and of work, and to other abuses of human rights.
repere.source: Domestic Workers Convention, 2011 (No. 189), Preamble, International Labour Organization

carte.punch: Only in 2011 does domestic work enter international labor law
carte.idee: Convention No. 189 of the International Labour Organization, adopted in 2011, guarantees household workers for the first time the same fundamental rights as other employees, from whom work in a private home had long excluded them.

quiz.question: What does ILO Convention No. 189 (2011) concretely bring to domestic workers compared with the earlier situation?
choix: It creates a specific international minimum wage, applied uniformly in all countries that ratify it
It recognizes for them the same fundamental rights as other employees, from whom work done in a private home had often excluded them
It now bans all recruitment of domestic workers from another country
It transfers responsibility for inspecting domestic work from states to the International Labour Organization itself
quiz.explication: Before 2011, work done in a private home often remained outside the scope of the laws that organize ordinary labor law. The convention requires states that ratify it to guarantee domestic workers freedom of association, the prohibition of forced labor and of the worst forms of child labor, and non-discrimination, as for other employees.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which country is the first to ratify Convention No. 189 on domestic work?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Uruguayan Parliament approves the convention on April 26, 2012, making Uruguay the first country to ratify it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What must Article 8 of Convention No. 189 guarantee to domestic workers recruited in one country to work in another?
choix: A work visa issued directly by the International Labour Organization
A written job offer even before crossing the border
A minimum wage identical to that of the country of origin
An automatic right to the host country's citizenship after one year
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 8 requires, for migrant domestic workers, a written job offer even before they cross the border.
